en: The *Prāṇābharaṇa*, composed by Paṇḍitarāja Śrī Jagannātha, together with the commentary (*ṭippaṇī*) written by him:
On this earth, scholars are mute in the praise of others' words; kings are reeling with intoxication from the swelling pride of the sport of wealth.

Whose mouth shall now taste the sweetness of my speech, which, imitating the loveliness of the lips of a celestial maiden languid with passion, is itself languid with love? 1.1 JPrā 1.1.1 JPrā 1.1.2 JPrā 1.1.3 JPrā 1.1.4 JPrā 1.1.5 JPrā 1.1.6 JPrā 1.1.7 JPrā 1.1.8 JPrā 1.1.9 JPrā 1.1.10 JPrā 1.1.11 JPrā 1.1.12 JPrā 1.1.13 JPrā 1.1.14 JPrā 1.1.15 JPrā 1.1.16 JPrā 1.1.17 JPrā 1.1.18 JPrā 1.1.19 JPrā 1.1.20 JPrā 1.1.21 JPrā 1.1.22 JPrā 1.1.23 JPrā 1.1.24 JPrā 1.1.25 JPrā 1.1.26 JPrā 1.1.27 JPrā 1.1.28 JPrā 1.1.29 JPrā 1.1.30 JPrā 1.1.31 JPrā 1.1.32 JPrā 1.1.33 JPrā 1.1.34 JPrā 1.1.35 JPrā 1.1.36 JPrā 1.1.37 JPrā 1.1.38 JPrā 1.1.39 JPrā 1.1.40 JPrā 1.1.41 JPrā 1.1.42 JPrā 1.1.43 JPrā 1.1.44 JPrā 1.1.45 JPrā 1.1.46 JPrā 1.1.47 JPrā 1.1.48 JPrā 1.1.49 JPrā 1.1.50 JPrā 1.1.51 JPrā 1.1.52 JPrā 1.1.53 JPrā 1.1.54 JPrā 1.1.55 JPrā 1.1.56 JPrā 1.1.57 JPrā 1.1.58 JPrā 1.1.59 JPrā 1.1.60 JPrā 1.1.61 JPrā 1.1.62 JPrā 1.1.63 JPrā 1.1.64 JPrā 1.1.65 JPrā 1.1.66 JPrā 1.1.67 JPrā 1.1.68 JPrā 1.1.69 JPrā 1.1.70 JPrā 1.1.71 JPrā 1.1.72 JPrā 1.1.73 JPrā 1.1.74 JPrā 1.1.75 JPrā 1.1.76 JPrā 1.1.77 JPrā 1.1.78 JPrā 1.1.79 JPrā 1.1.80 JPrā 1.1.81 JPrā 1.1.82 JPrā 1.1.83 JPrā 1.1.84 JPrā 1.1.85 JPrā 1.1.86 JPrā 1.1.87 JPrā 1.1.88 JPrā 1.1.89 JPrā 1.1.90 JPrā 1.1.91 JPrā 1.1.92 JPrā 1.1.93 JPrā 1.1.94 JPrā 1.1.95 JPrā 1.1.96 JPrā 1.1.97 JPrā 1.1.98 JPrā 1.1.99
The phrase "the learned," and so forth, is intended to indicate what is generally observed.
Therefore, those with aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdayas) should not be even slightly discouraged.
Furthermore, this is an instance of the suggestion of a state of being (bhāvadhvani).
Because the poet’s thought— characterized by the experience of employing this verse and having as its object the meaning to be established in the second half— is primarily manifested here,
there is the distinct ornament of *vyatireka* (distinction), where both causes are not explicitly stated.
[The state of being languid with passion] belongs to the beautiful woman, while the excellence of the sweetness of the lower lip belongs to the [lover].
Appreciation for merit has utterly vanished, the burden of envy has increased greatly, and this Kali age has arrived, filling the very womb of the world’s beauty.
O my poetry, why do you resort to silence with such a thought? May the illustrious Lord of Kāmarūpa awaken and remain here on the circle of the earth for a long time!
This is also a suggestion (*dhvani*) of the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the king, who is the object of the poet's internal state.
From here onwards, this very [suggestion] will persist until the final verse.

And here, the despondency (*nirveda*)—which has silence as its manifesting sign (*anubhāva*) and the king as its objective basis (*ālambana*)—is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), serving as the locus for the *preyas* ornament.

And here, in the case of insentient poetry, what is intended is the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of a relation where there is no relation, rooted in the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of sentience [in that which is actually insentient].
Therefore, there is no inconsistency regarding the invocation of *bhāvanā*, silence, despondency, and the act of addressing.

The thundering roar of the pair of drums prevails throughout the world—a sound as deep as it would disdain the rumbling of clouds rising at the time of universal dissolution at the moment of your departure; a sound heard by lions emerging from the depths of their mountain caves with the corners of their eyes flickering in anger at the offense of being awakened from sleep, and which has rubbed against the shores of the Milky Ocean.

In this instance, because the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of enthusiasm (*utsāha*) residing in the lion— which is supported by the king, ignited by hearing such a roar, manifested through the movement of his eyes, and nourished by the transitory emotion (*saṃcāribhāva*) of indignation revealed by his leaping into the interior of the mountain cave— is subordinate to the emotion of love (*rati*) directed toward the king, it constitutes the figure of speech known as *rasālaṃkāra*.
As they say:
"In that poem where rasa and the like are subordinate to another sentence-meaning as its primary element, my view is that rasa and the like constitute a mere ornament (alaṃkāra)."
Thus [it is said].
However, in the third and fourth quarters, the excellence of the contrast (*vyatireka*) is indeed manifest.
By the word "rubbed" (*ghṛṣṭa*), it is implied that such a sound did not proceed further because it was obstructed by the coastal mountains.
Otherwise, it would follow that [the sun] might even touch the Lokāloka mountain;
thus, it is understood that [the text] did not say "polished" (*mṛṣṭa*).
For if that were the case, it would result in the impression of laxity.
O Indra of the Earth, what can we say of your heroism, when you— whose brows are arched in play and whose eyes are red—

behold your circle of arms adorned with thousands of ornaments, their brilliance jagged with the luster of rows of rubies, while at that very moment the trees of the mountain caves and forest dwellings of the Vindhya range are set ablaze?

In this context, by means of the irrelevant ornamentation and activity of the cave-dwellings and trees situated in the Vindhya forest— whether those in caves or those in the wilds— the [poet describes] your enemies' wives who, having abandoned their own cities, have at night deposited all their ornaments in cave-dwellings and at the foot of trees, and having made their beds there, are now in a state of agitation due to the news of your arrival in the morning.

The forgetfulness of that action, or its abandonment due to the weight [of the burden], is understood as being introduced; thus, this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). However, when the effect is somehow introduced, the ornament is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
"The ultimate limit of my greatness is my own home; my father is the very embodiment of profundity; I alone am the sole possessor of jewels in this world—what other like me could there be?
Having reflected thus, O Ocean of Milk, do not suddenly fall into the darkness of pride; for the illustrious Prāṇanārāyaṇa reigns supreme, equal to you.

In this context, there is a variety of the figure *pratīpa* (the inverse simile), which consists of a similarity being described in order to set aside the excellence based on the absence of similarity caused by the specific qualities of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Some maintain that this is merely a particular type of *upamā* (simile);
others hold that it is a distinct figure altogether due to its unique aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*).

O Lord, your fame—whose soul is immersed in the moonlight emanating from the body of the one who bears the moon as his crest-jewel, which sports together with the lovely circles of waves of the Ocean of Milk, which dwells upon the sandy banks of the celestial river, and which converses with the rays of the nectar-moon—why does it not attain the highest degree of brilliance? 6.
In this context, the subject matter of *samāsa* (compression) is that the excellence of whiteness in the fame is stated as being caused by its connection with its substratum [the moon].

The subject matter of *sāra* (culmination) is that the excellence residing in the king is perceived as being successively augmented—by the cloth upon the moon, by that [moon] upon the Blessed One, and by the Blessed One upon the king—in this manner: "the cloth [is white], the moon [is white], the Blessed One [is white], and the king [is white]."
You bind up your curls, you cast off your white upper garment out of a longing for pleasure, you bring about the subjugation of Laṅkā, and you inflict wounds upon your thighs and forehead;
O King, alas, you embrace every limb with merciless caresses—wondrous indeed is your audacity regarding the objects of women!

In this [figure], there is *śleṣa* (punning) between two narratives—one relevant and one irrelevant—both of which reside in the subject (*prakṛti-dharmin*), or between two narratives that are both relevant.
This [punning] occurs in six instances: it is based on a multiplicity of words in two cases, and based on a multiplicity of meanings in four cases.
The ancients maintain that both of these are figures of sound (*śabdālaṃkāra*).

The moderns maintain that the first is a verbal figure (śabdālaṅkāra) because of the joining of words according to the analogy of lac and wood, whereas the second is a semantic figure (arthālaṅkāra) because of the joining of meanings according to the analogy of two fruits on a single stalk.

O Lord, let the sages praise you from all sides; what is the use of that? For how could you truly be worthy of praise merely by that? Rather, you are to be praised because the youthful majesty of your bow constantly holds the earth within its embrace, embraces the quarters, kisses the heavens, and suddenly reaches even the inaccessible city of Amarāvatī.

Here, the connection with the earth and so forth, which has reached its full manifestation, exists as non-different from the story of a lover revealed by common attributes delimited by specific marks; thus, this is *samāsokti* (condensed expression), which proceeds by relying on the similarity of attributes through pure commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) brought about by the nature of the effect.
And because it gives rise to censure, it is a subordinate element (*guṇa*) within *avyājastuti* (feigned praise).
"O King, do not succumb to pride because of the trivial prattle of the dull-witted who say, 'You shake off the calamities of the worlds and bring about most exalted prosperity.
Alas, your beloved Fame, having compressed even your exceedingly lofty body into the interior of this tiny vessel of the universe, dwells there with great difficulty."
In this case as well, it is as before;

however, because it results in the establishment of the greater extent of either the locus or the located through the conceptualization of the lesser extent of the other, the figure of speech *sādhikā* is also a quality (*guṇa*) in that [type of *atiśayokti*].
"O Lord, how are we to believe your bold declaration that while you rule the earth, not even a trace of calamity shall befall anyone?
For it is evident before our eyes that as the hosts of your enemies fly into the sky in a rage, the Sun—the primordial progenitor of your lineage—is being pierced by them."
But here, that [vyājastuti] is indeed not embraced by either *adhika* or *samāsokti*.

Through relish comes flavor; through flavor, poetry; through poetry, eloquence; through that, the connoisseur who delights in the aesthetic essence (rasa) within the hearts of people; through him, the assembly;

and through the assembly, O Lord of the Earth, you—who are like a raincloud pouring down streams of nectar upon this world scorched by the fire of poverty—and through you, the entire circle of the earth shines resplendent. (JPran 11)
The ancients maintain that this is *mālādīpaka* (the "garland-lamp" figure).
However, we hold that since *dīpaka* is necessarily rooted in similarity (*sādṛśya*), this cannot be *mālādīpaka*, but rather a variety of *ekāvalī* (the "single-string" figure).
O Lord, since the night-lotuses of your enemies have withered away, the clusters of darkness in the form of their wretchedness have swiftly perished on all sides,
the paths of the righteous are spreading wide, and the lotuses of the virtuous are attaining full bloom— I believe that the sun of your majesty’s prowess is now intent upon its rising.

In this case, since the mark (liṅga) is produced by a metaphor (rūpaka), and because poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is impossible due to the absence of a cause (nimitta), the word "anumāna" refers to inference (anumiti).

As the beautiful women of your rival kings flee into the thickets, what trees are there that do not strike them with haste? Some uproot their heavy braided hair; some turn them toward both sides; some press down upon the pair of their lotus-feet; and others, in their rage, cast aside the hem of their garments far away. (JPran 13)

In this case, because the gathering of hair into a braid (*kabara*) and other such actions are mixed with thorns due to their commonality, there occurs a *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) which proceeds by relying on the similarity of the qualifiers through a pure commonality that is unmixed with any other property of the effect.
O King, your gaze is filled with auspiciousness and composed of Mercury; your assembly is the abode of Kāvya (Śukra); your beautiful lower lip is the support of Aruṇa (the Sun);
your anger is the thunderbolt; O you of vast intellect, your heart is the seat of Soma (the Moon); and indeed, O King of undiminished prowess, you are the refuge of all the planets.

Here, since the object— the king— is the substratum for the superimposed state of being the locus of all planetary influences (*sarvagrahālambanatva*) among the co-located attributes (*samānādhikaraṇa-dharma*) which have as their constituent parts those respective planets, there is a convergence of the commonality of those attributes through the device of producing non-difference by means of *śleṣa* (punning) between the qualifying planets and the qualifiers such as "auspiciousness" (*kalyāṇa*) and so forth; thus, the establishment of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on that [convergence] is achieved.
In the past, at the beginning of creation, you indeed performed a fierce and merciless penance with rays of fire blazing like matted locks in order to protect the circle of the world;
yet now, with eyes red with fury and desiring to set out upon the battlefield, we realize, alas, that the illustrious Lord of Kāmarūpa was not known by you.

In this instance, while the sun is the subject under description as a means for generating fear in the context of praising the king, its direct departure—which is not inherently conducive to that purpose—is superseded by the effect of "piercing the solar orb" performed by the enemy; this latter effect is directly conducive to the intended purpose and is thus understood through the figure of Aprastutapraśaṃsā.

Having come from the abode of the Lotus-Seated One to behold the surface of the three worlds, and having spent some days among the gods, O King— O abode of truth— the Goddess of Speech, who is worshipped by the assembly of great poets, has now returned out of curiosity to wander the circle of the earth and dwells happily within your lotus-like mouth.
Here, *paryāya* (sequential occurrence) arises because a single thing to be contained (*ādheya*) is related to multiple loci (*ādhāra*).

In this context, the locus mentioned in the first quarter of the verse is understood through implication (*ākṣepa*), since the fifth case (*pañcamī*) expressing separation (*viśleṣa*) presupposes proximity (*upaśleṣa*), which constitutes the locative of proximity (*aupaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*).

By means of the identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (paranomasia), the status of the face as the "World of Truth" (*satyaloka*) is established; once that is established, the establishment of its being a place for happy dwelling follows.

Is he the most profound weapon of the learned, or perhaps the forest fire for the jungle of the lineage of enemy kings; is he, oh wonder, an ocean of milk for the moon of his brilliantly shining fame, or is he a life-restoring medicine for women bitten by the serpent of the bodiless Love? To which men does this lord of men not produce such manifold conceptions? (JPran 17)

In this case, because the superimpositions of the various "ends" (koṭis) are rooted in further superimpositions, there is a "successive doubt" (paramparita-saṃśaya), and that is "volitional" (āhārya),
since the root superimposition is of that nature;
for there is no contradiction in having a volitional cognition even in another cognizer constructed by the poet, just as in the case of the poet himself.
The rutting elephants trumpet, the throngs of horses neigh loudly, and the bards recite hymns of praise in the temple honored by your eulogies;
yet this shall remain so, O Lord, only as long as that red glow from the corners of your eyes—which resembles the fire at the end of an aeon—has not increased.

In this instance, the comparison of the red glow of the corner of the eye to the fire at the end of an eon— which assists the primary meaning, namely the poet’s devotion directed toward the king— is a *vastūpakāriṇī* (an embellishment that assists the matter), because it serves to support the fact that "the very moment your anger arises, the wealth of your enemies will be reduced to ashes."

O Lord of the Earth, do not be angry with me for remaining silent while I am engaged in composing a likeness of you; think not that this poet does not describe me, for in the mind of the Creator who brought forth this world of moving and unmoving beings, there is certainly no other man equal to you, let alone a second.

Regarding this, the ancients held that because of the cognition "there is no one else equal to you," this is a case where the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is elided, and thus it is a suggested simile (*vyaṅgya-upamā*).
However, this is not a simile at all, because in every respect the similarity is not established;
otherwise, it would follow that even a contrast (*vyatireka*) would possess the nature of a simile.
"Searching through the Ketaka groves filled with thorns, you will perish;
O bee, as you wander, you shall not obtain that which is like the flower of the Mālatī."

However, in this case, since it is understood from the statement "you shall not obtain [it]" that it will exist in some place beyond your reach, let it be a *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) based on the establishment of similarity.
Therefore, the moderns maintain that this is indeed the figure of speech *asamālaṅkāra* (the unequal).
O destroyer of the circle of enemies, as he beheld you in battle— tearing apart proud elephants with the *paṭṭiśa* brandished by your arms—
whose heart did not instantly leap up at the sight of the enemy of Jambha, who had split the Vindhya mountain asunder with the blow of his formidable thunderbolt?
Here, however, the figure of speech *smaraṇa* (recollection) is the intended subject.
You are Yama for rival kings, Agni for those dwelling in your realm, Yudhiṣṭhira for the virtuous, and the Lord of Wealth for those desiring riches;
you alone on this earth have been fashioned by the Creator in many forms as a home constructed with the tips of thunderbolts for those seeking refuge. JPran 21.

In this verse, because the poet fashions the king—who is already possessed of beauty—into the form of Yama and so forth, there is a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification); and because, upon his arrival, there arises the possibility of an illusion (*bhrānti*) on the part of rival kings and others that he is indeed Yama and the like, there is a *bhrāntimad* (illusion) figure; furthermore, because he is depicted through multiple attributes by those same multiple perceivers, there is a specific type of *ullekha* (multiple description).

Thus, although it is intermingled with these, it is primarily an *ullekha* characterized by the multiplicity of the subject being described, as prompted by the various distinctions expressed in the genitive case denoting relationship.

Like Indra with two eyes, like the sun with measured rays, like a second moon, like the god of love incarnate, like the ocean in human form, and like the Preceptor descended upon earth for the sake of forbearance—may the Lord of Kāmarūpa, praised by all the gods, be victorious! (JPran 22)

Here, in order to remove the contradiction between the king’s attributes—such as having two eyes—which are opposed to his identity with Indra and the others, those attributes are made common by superimposing [the attributes] upon the subjects, namely Indra and the rest; thus, there is a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on that, and it takes the form of a garland (*mālārūpā*).
Furthermore, a simile (*upamā*) is not possible here in its literal sense.
Otherwise, the reasoning regarding [the Lord] having two eyes and so forth would result in being purposeless.
Nor is their commonality (sādhāraṇya) the producer of the simile, because even in its absence, that simile is accomplished through such qualities as supreme sovereignty which are perceived;
furthermore, because it is unpoetic, it is not intended by the poet as a producer of a simile.
In this way, the superimposition of the moon and so forth upon the second [face] and the others would likewise be entirely purposeless, even if there were a simile.

O King, your manifold mental disposition has been charming from birth: it is moist with compassion toward the multitude of the wretched, yet merciless toward the entire host of enemies; it is gentle in poetic discourse, yet maintains harshness in the formulation of logical rebuttals; it is greedy for dharma, yet not greedy for wealth; and it is ever-fleeing at the sight of another's misfortune. (JPran 23)
In this context, the mention is that the mental state (cittavṛtti) is of many kinds due to its being directed toward multiple objects;
and in that regard, the determination of it as a single unit is based on its being a single mental state belonging to that [subject].

"O King, who are these gods, and who are these former gods? Who among the men in this assembly are speaking thus before you? As long as the serpent of your sword—whose form is like the terrifying weapon of Death, whose smooth luster is the milk-drinker for the lives of foolish enemies—does not come within the range of my vision, so long do these warrior-kṣatriyas remain as if they were hosts of opposing armies. (JPran 24)
Here, there is a pure serial metaphor (*śuddhaparamparitarūpaka*).

O Embellisher of the Earth, that splendor of crimson in your eyes during battle shines forth like the beauty of the ruby of the sun as it rises at the morning twilight; it is like the terrifying garland of flames of the fire of wrath that devours the world; and it possesses the luster of beautiful lac-dye trickling from the soles of the lotus-feet of the beloved of the quarters. JPran_25 //
In this case as well, it is that very same [nature], but it consists of a series.
Beholding you in battle— the sole connoisseur in banishing the pride of harsh fortitude from the ranks of beautiful women— alas,
which royal fortune among the enemy kings maintained its unswerving devotion to her husband?
In this case, the intended meaning—that the royal fortune of the enemies has come to you—is expressed in the form of a lapse in her devotion to her husband; thus, it is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
And since that requires *samāsokti* (condensed expression) for the purpose of establishing the royal fortune as a heroine (*nāyikā*), the latter serves as an excellence (*guṇa*) in that context.
When truthfulness resides in his speech, Arjuna in his fame, Dharma in his actions,
and the source of the life-breath of the world in his mind, how much more so must the sons of Pāṇḍu be under his control?

Here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the sons of Pāṇḍu as being identical with their subjection to the king, the attribute of the superimposed object (*viṣayin*), namely "being dependent on the king," is made common to the objects (*viṣaya*) through *śleṣa* (punning) by effecting an identity between those objects and their dependents— namely, Untruth, Non-existence, Whiteness, Virtue, and the Supreme Lord.
O Lord, the Creator fashioned your compassionate glances from the nectar-fragments that arose from the Ocean of Milk when it was subjected to the force of the churning of Mount Mandara,
which then attained unity with various medicinal herbs.

Here, at the ends of the verses, the poet does not intend to convey only qualities such as reviving the dead, which are the exclusive attributes of nectar; rather, he intends others as well, such as the power to subjugate all people. Thus, the association with medicinal herbs is mentioned in the drops of ambrosia for the sake of poetic excellence (atiśaya).
In battle, you, merciless as you were, swiftly and forcefully drew the string of your bow together with the hair of the women, the treasures of all the rival kings, and their very lives.

And here, there is a *sahokti* (joint description) enlivened by an excellence consisting in the reversal of the sequence of actions such as pulling the hair and so forth, which are acts of drawing away.
Let poets call you equal to Mahendra; what can we do to prevent that here?
For how could you, being attended by thousands, be the same as the Lord of the Thirty-three?
Here, taking up the number "thirty-three" (tridaśatva) suggested by the pun (*śleṣa*), a contrast (*vyatireka*) is established based on both causes.
May that cloud-pourer rain down water; you, O noble-minded one, rain down jewels.
He is stained by the night of the new moon, while you here are pure both within and without.

In this case as well, it is that very same [type of simile], but the distinction is that here the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) does not trigger the comparison, and the similarity being negated is not expressed by words (*śābda*).
By some he was determined to be a lord of men; by others he was proclaimed a lord of wealth;
yet he became on earth solely a lord of speech, while in his own mind he was a lord of the god of love alone.
Here, there is the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment), consisting of the form "this is not a king, but rather the Lord of Speech.
In this instance, the negative aspect is understood from the first half-verse through the statement of the ultimate reality,
while the aspect of superimposition (*āropa*) is conveyed by the second half-verse.
Endowed with great warriors resembling sea-monsters and with poets like jewels, you, O jewel among kings,
are here the vessel for both the nectar of poetry and the moon of fame.

In this case, although the comparison of the king to the ocean is expressed by the word itself, because it is implied through the comparisons of its constituent parts (*aṅga-upamā*), it is an *ekadeśavivartinī* (partially manifest) simile; therefore, in the second half-verse, there is only a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of that which is compared).
This is because the identity (*tādātmya*) to be understood from a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (attributive compound) is of no use in the present context.
O Lord of the Earth, before the enemy kings have even come before you, they are reduced to mere ashes;
immediately thereafter, sparks from the fire of your wrath fall from the arches of your knitted brows.
In this instance, the excellence of speed in the one being prompted (the *prayojya*) is understood as being produced by the excellence of the prompter (*prayojaka*).
And this is a case of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting in the reversal of the temporal sequence between cause and effect.
O King, even if the three worlds were filled with humans, gods, and demons,
there has never been, is not, and will never be anyone who can equal you.
Regarding this, the ancients maintain that it is a "deficient simile" (luptopamā) lacking the standard of comparison;
however, we consider it to be a distinct ornament (alaṃkāra) called the "unequal" (asamākhya).
For those who have drunk even a small portion of your speech, which is like nectar-soup,
the overflowing sweetness of the bimba-fruit lips of women is no longer sufficient for their satisfaction.

In this connection, there is also the variety of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) known as "non-connection where there is a connection. Furthermore, there is *vyatireka* (contrast), which consists in a distinction characterized by the thought: "If even a small amount of sweetness is unable to achieve equality with a large amount when both are compared through the qualifiers of the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), then what need is there to mention the case of a larger amount? Thus, it takes the form of a disparity.
Your fame, abiding in the sky, illuminates the entire world and causes the night-lotuses to bloom; having reached the earth, it renders the labors of Sagara’s sons fruitless.
Here, there is a suggestion of *ullekha* (multiple description) intermingled with the metaphor of "manifest moonlight."
O ruler of the earth, you rise from your seat together with Fortune, possessed by pride;
yet you fall upon them all at once along with Death.
In the phrase "by the hair of the brides," there is a mention of the object (*karman*) in conjunction [with the instrument];
here, however, the distinction is that it is the agent (*kartṛ*) who is so mentioned.
While you, who are equal to Indra, the subduer of Pāka, rule over the entire circle of the earth,
the eyes and the days alike rain down upon the forests of your enemies' wives.

Here, because of the pun (*śleṣa*) based on the *kvip*-suffix in the sense of "acting like rain" (*varṣavat ācaranti*), there is a figure of speech rooted in punning known as *tulyayogitā* (Equal Treatment).
This is because both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) are equally contextual (*prakṛta*), as they both pertain to the description of the enemy's beloved.
O Lord of Men, for one who holds in the palm of his hand the medicine that eliminates all harm,
how could there be any fear of snakes even as he wanders over the entire earth?

Here, because the superimposition of identity with a remedy (*bheṣaja*) upon the king— which is employed as the means of establishing the absence of fear of snakes indicated by *śleṣa*— also serves as a means of establishing the identity between the quality of "removing enemies" residing in the king and the quality of "causing distress to snakes" indicated by *śleṣa*,
there is a *śliṣṭa-paramparita-rūpaka* (compound-based transposed metaphor) in the first quarter; however, in the third quarter, there is *śleṣa* alone.
What wonder is there that your fame steals away the splendor of the blue lotus?
For its cause is indeed you, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the world.

Here, because the produced [object] possesses qualities identical to those of the producer, there is a specific type of simile (samālaṃkāra) corresponding to the connection between the producer and the produced;
and *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is the poetic quality (*guṇa*) in this case.
If fierce moonlight, sandalwood, and moonbeams are seen in the assembly hall,
then you are gentle in battle, yet possess weapons like the fire at the end of time.

In this regard, because the word "you" (*tvam*) is elided from the sentence "seen here in the assembly," and because the word "you" is carried over (*anuvartana*) in the sentence "then you are the agreement," there is the figure of speech *padavinimaya* (exchange of words) in the first half-verse.
In the second half-verse, there is *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), due to the connection with several attributes pertaining to the subject at hand.

The intermingling [of figures] consists of another poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) characterized by the attribution of qualities contrary to those of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), for the purpose of establishing the superior quality of the object compared (*upameya*).
In this shoreless saṃsāra, O King, by fate only one Arjuna was created;
but by you, through your stainless fame, all have been made Arjunas.
In this case, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) is rooted in *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
In Dadhīci, Bali, Karṇa, the Himalayas, the Golden Mountain, and the oceans,
non-generosity and lack of fortitude appear only when they are actually observed.
In this case as well, it is that very same [type],
though the distinction lies in the commingling according to their respective order.
O King, while you rule over the entire circle of the earth,
there is not even the slightest anxiety within the circle of either enemies or friends.
Here too, there is *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), and *vyājastuti* (ironical praise) arising from the pun on the word *mittra*.
"Is this Bhānu, Agni, Yama, Vāyu, Bali, Karṇa, or Śibi?"—in this way, your adversaries are conceived as supplicants within you. (JPran 46)
But here, however, doubt is characterized by the mention of alternatives.
You, who are a lake for the dwelling of Kamalā, a lordly serpent for patience and fortitude,
and the moon for the blue water-lily, bring joy to all human beings.
Here, the *śliṣṭa-paramparita-rūpaka* (conjoined sequential metaphor) takes the form of a garland (*mālā*).
O Protector of the Earth, your glories act as moonlight in the sky, act as snow upon the Himalayas,
and act as oceans upon the earth.
In this case, the figure of speech *ullekha* (multiple description) is embraced by *mālōpamā* (garland simile).
O King, among deer you are the lion, among trees you are the sandalwood, and among rulers you are the moon; thus, O Lord of the Earth, you are Indra.

Here, there is a pure serial simile (śuddhaparamparitā mālārūpopamā) consisting of forms derived from a verbal root ending in the *kvip* suffix followed by the suffix *śatṛ*, and one form in the *tiṅ* (finite verb) [ending in *indavasi*].
In the center of the nectar-ocean, within a palace made of white crystal,
upon a seat of the full moon, O Lord, your words are worthy to abide.

Here, since the sweetness of the three—the ocean of nectar and the others—has reached its highest pitch through the relationship of qualifier and qualified, it is appropriate for them to be connected with the words of your speech, and not to remain disjointed; thus, this is *prauḍhokti* (bold assertion) based on the employment of hyperbolic qualifiers.

O Lord, how can this mass of light, most fierce and filled with the network of flames from the fire of universal destruction, surpass You—who have eclipsed the moonlight of the nectar-waves and the lotus-face of the Goddess Rāmā, and who are a great ocean of boundless grace? (JPran 51)
In this instance, there is the figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous), because an effect arises possessing qualities contrary to those of its cause.

Through the *vyatireka* (distinction) consisting in the surpassing of the three—namely, the waves of nectar and so forth—the excellence of [the speaker’s] qualities of being life-giving, supremely cooling, pure, and beautiful is understood.
Thus, although other figures of speech are also present in these verses, they have not been analyzed here due to their obviousness.

Out of affection for those with sensitive hearts (sahṛdayas), a certain portion has necessarily been explained; however, the rest should be brought forth by them themselves, so enough of this prolixity.

The illustrious Paṇḍitarāja Paṇḍita Jagannātha—delighted by the compassion of Mahālakṣmī, the auspicious abode of the Tailaṅga lineage; the son of the venerable Peramabhaṭṭa; who constantly scorches the foreheads of the learned; and who was thoroughly pleased upon hearing the poetry of the Lord of Kamatā—composed this description of him. (JPran 52)
O Lord of the Earth, beholding you here in the midst of battle—with your two staff-like arms wielding a shimmering bow that has destroyed the circle of arrogant enemies with fierce arrows;

and seeing the son of Pāṇḍu enraged at the Khāṇḍava forest, his dance of destruction performed by the circles of flames from the volleys of arrows released from the leaping Gāṇḍīva—who would not remember [the Lord]? 53.
Here, the figure of speech is *smaraṇālaṃkāra* (remembrance).

One should not, however, be misled by the term *bhāva* (emotional state); for in this context, the distinction between *bhāva* and *alaṃkāra* is established by whether they are rooted in similarity (*sādṛśya*) or not, and because [the latter] is cognizable through words (*śabdavedyatva*).
Thus ends the *Prāṇābharaṇa*, composed by Paṇḍitarāja Śrī Jagannātha, together with the commentary (*ṭippaṇī*) written by the same author.
